result.summary: This surface of google.golang.org/protobuf v1.36.11 is the official Go protobuf runtime: wire encode/decode, reflection, legacy message support, lazy decoding, and the embedded edition-defaults blob parsed at init. I checked the init code, the embedded binary's consumer, environment reads, and the reflection/unsafe uses. All match upstream behaviour, with no network, process execution, file writes, secret access or hidden payloads.

findings.title: Embedded binary edition defaults
findings.detail: editiondefaults embeds a 154-byte binary FeatureSetDefaults protobuf, which upstream generates from protoc. It is consumed only by filedesc.unmarshalEditionDefaults at init. That parser accepts a fixed set of field numbers, panics on anything unknown, and only sets boolean/int feature flags in a defaults cache. It cannot carry executable content or change behaviour beyond protobuf edition defaults.

findings.title: Environment variable toggles lazy decoding
findings.detail: An init-time read of GOPROTODEBUG=nolazy disables lazy unmarshalling. This is a documented upstream debug knob that only selects between eager and lazy decoding paths. It does not affect security.

findings.title: Init functions are benign
findings.detail: filedesc and proto have init functions. They parse the embedded edition defaults, set surrogate file features, and assign proto.Error. None has side effects outside process memory.

capabilities.explanation: Comes from reflection and unsafe pointer arithmetic, which is how the protobuf runtime reaches generated message structs. Method.Func.Call is used on XXX_OneofFuncs, XXX_OneofWrappers and ExtensionRangeArray methods of generated or legacy message types. reflect.NewAt, unsafe.Pointer offsets and atomic pointer operations implement fast field access. Legacy Marshal/Unmarshal/Merge interface methods are called on user message types. Only the program's own compiled-in types are invoked; nothing is loaded or run from data.

There is no network code in the package: no net, net/http or socket use. The capability is most likely an artifact of call-graph analysis through interface dispatch: legacyMarshaler/legacyUnmarshaler/legacyMerger interface calls and reflect Method.Func.Call can, in theory, reach any method in the binary, including networking types. In practice these calls only serialize, parse and merge messages in memory.
